Pencil

A declarative language for mathematical figures. A figure is a text file that says what’s in it and what each thing means, and style sheets say how it looks. The same file renders as an interactive figure on the web and as video.

It’s early, and the syntax will change. Pencil is being built to make math explainers, one real figure at a time, and nothing about the language is stable yet.

Styling a figure

A document names things and says what they are. This one says there’s a curve c, the points at distance r from the origin, and that r breathes with time. It holds no colors and no sizes.

A sheet targets the name c. Because the curve is implicit, it has a signed distance, so a sheet can style its inside and outside. The second sheet bands both sides by that distance and moves the hue with time, and not a line of the document changes.

What’s in it

  • Mathematical expressions.Points are complex numbers, derivatives are exact, and a solve can find unknowns each frame. A figure compiles to an IR with its expressions in MathJSON, so it isn’t locked into this tool.
  • Animation and interaction.Both bind the params of one figure, so what a reader drags and what a video plays are the same description.
  • Collections and maps.One declaration can draw thousands of dots, circles or curves, and can go through a function, so one thing can appear in several panels.
  • Strokes and sides.A circle has a handedness and can straighten into a line and turn over, and both of its sides can be drawn at once. A taper can follow arc length.
  • Style sheets.A figure holds no colors, sizes or renderer-specific calls. Styles target its names, with CSS-like rules and math-specific properties.
  • Rendering and checking.A Rust core compiles figures to WGSL for WebGPU and WebGL2, and a separate CPU interpreter defines what each pixel should be. pencil check compares them.

Where it stands

Pencil is built from a corpus of real figures, and a feature goes in only when a figure needs it. The syntax and the IR change freely while that goes on, so expect files written today to need edits later.

Figures here are drawn on your GPU, through WebGPU where the browser has it and WebGL2 otherwise. They’ve been checked mostly in Chrome on a Mac; other browsers and phones much less. If a figure doesn’t draw, the page says why under it.

Pencil is early, and its syntax will change. Source on GitHub, under the MIT license.
